schools.summary: Ellicott and Keil set the scene and the Persian dating: Nisan still falls in the twentieth year because the record adopts Persian reckoning, the reign beginning before Chisleu.
Henry reads the four-month delay as prudence, not sloth — prayer must be seconded with endeavour; winter was unfit and his month of waiting had not come.
Wesley lays the delay to his turn of service or a fit opportunity; Clarke adds the Persian custom of a cup-bearer for each quarter of the year, now come to Nehemiah's turn.
Gill fixes the chronology (Jewish year from Nisan, others from Tisri) and supposes the interval spent in fasting and prayer.

Keil renders the king's diagnosis, 'sorrow of heart,' and the accustomed 'let the king live for ever'; Ellicott traces the fear to the abrupt inquiry, since a sad face was never tolerated before even the milder Artaxerxes.
Clarke suspects the king feared treachery or remorse; Wesley grounds the dread in the great and invidious request, odious to the courtiers, and the fear of a refusal.
Henry names fear of the king's wrath or of misspeaking, praises humble self-diffidence, and commends the king's Christian sympathy with a servant's grief.
Gill notes there was no bodily disorder to explain the change in Nehemiah's face, which prompts the king's question.

sides.position: the king suspected some treachery or bad design behind the sad face
the suddenness of the inquiry, a sad countenance being intolerable in the royal presence
the greatness and invidiousness of his request and the fear of a refusal
fear of the king's wrath, or of losing the suit by an ill-chosen word

schools.summary: Clarke reads 'let the king live for ever' as a disclaimer of ill-will, citing Aelian on Artaxerxes Mnemon; Wesley notes Nehemiah names only the sepulchres, not the temple, before a heathen king.
Ellicott: Nehemiah's family was of Jerusalem; he hides his deepest desire and pleads the desecrated sepulchres, an appeal of great force with tomb-revering Persians.
Gill takes the blessing both as common salutation and as a stroke to allay any suspicion of a design on the king's life.
Henry vindicates the grief — 'I do well to be sad' — and makes the ruins of the church a fit matter of sorrow to every public-spirited soul.

outliers.note: Distinctively presses that Nehemiah said not a word of the temple, naming only the fathers' sepulchres, because he spoke before a heathen king who cared for none of these things.

themes: appeal to Persian reverence for tombs

schools.summary: Henry makes the secret ejaculation the hinge of the whole business — boldness given by the king's invitation, as Christ's invitation emboldens us to the throne of grace; solemn and sudden prayers each keep their place.
Keil sees the king already inclined to relieve Jerusalem, and Nehemiah praying to secure divine help; Ellicott calls it the first note of the book's characteristic ejaculatory prayer.
Clarke: mental prayer, for 'to the spirit of prayer every place is a praying place'; Wesley: he prayed to guide his own words and to incline the king's heart.
Gill: the king, reading meaning in the sad looks, encouraged his servant to name the favour he desired.

themes: the God of heaven above the monarch
boldness at the throne of grace

schools.summary: Keil sets out the request to be sent to Judah, to the city of his fathers' sepulchres, to build it, noting the conditional idiom of finding favour 'before' the king recurrent in Esther.
Clarke stresses the shrewdness: naming again the sacred sepulchres, Nehemiah touched a chord certain to move a tomb-revering Persian.
Gill notes he rests the whole petition on the king's pleasure and unmerited favour, not on any desert of his own.
Henry unfolds the vast content of the modest words — a governorship of twelve years, the wall's rebuilding, convoy and letters — granted not by interest but by the good hand of God.

themes: the good hand of God in the king's heart

schools.summary: Keil marks the shegal of Psalm 45 granting leave once the time was fixed; Ellicott identifies her as Damaspia the one legitimate queen and notes this was no public feast.
Clarke denies she was queen at all, taking shegal as chief concubine (with the LXX), not Esther; Wesley notes the queen's presence as unusual and supposes she promoted the request.
Gill sees providence in her good will to the Jews and guesses her Atossa, daughter of Cyrus, if the king were Darius Hystaspis.

debates.question: Who was the royal woman (shegal) sitting by the king?

sides.position: not a queen but the chief favourite or concubine
possibly Atossa, daughter of Cyrus, friendly to the Jews

schools.summary: Keil orders the requests for letters to the governors west of the Euphrates for safe passage; Ellicott notes protection was needed only beyond the river, not in the settled heart of the empire near Susa.
Gill identifies the 'river' as the Euphrates and the governors as those on its side toward Judah, through whose provinces the road ran.

themes: the captive made a royal envoy

schools.summary: Ellicott makes Asaph a Jew keeping a park near Jerusalem, the pardes ('paradise'), the beams for the temple fortress (later Antonia), the wall, and Nehemiah's house; Keil dwells on pardes as an Old Persian pleasure-ground.
Wesley takes the forest as Lebanon and the palace as the king's house adjoining the temple; Clarke traces pardes through Arabic and Greek, likening the royal forest to the New Forest or Windsor.
Gill takes Asaph's charge to be the forest of Lebanon, an orchard-like paradise, its keeper the Roman saltuarius.

debates.question: Where was the king's forest that supplied the timber?

sides.position: the forest of Lebanon, famous for its choice trees
an artificial park (pardes) near Jerusalem, kept by Asaph a Jew

themes: the temple fortress and the wall

schools.summary: Keil reads the captains and horsemen as a pluperfect ('had sent') and contrasts Nehemiah's accepted escort with Ezra, who was ashamed to ask one (Ezra 8:22).
Henry reads the escort as shield and honour, and an emblem that those whom the King of kings sends he protects with a host of attendant angels.
Gill leaves open whether these governors were the Tatnai and Shethar-boznai of some eighteen years before.

Keil marks the doubled Hebrew of their grief and the irony of 'a man to seek the welfare of Israel'; with Ellicott derives 'the Horonite' from Beth-horon in Samaria and makes Sanballat the Samaritan satrap, Tobiah his secretary.

Clarke makes Sanballat a Moabite of Horonaim governing the Samaritans and Tobiah an Ammonite joint-governor; Wesley reads 'the servant' as the low condition from which Tobiah was raised, hence his insolence.
Gill takes Sanballat as presiding at or sprung from Horonaim, a city of Moab.
Henry looks past geography to the malice: the enemies were galled to see the Jews cleared of slander and now trusted with a royal commission.

sides.position: from Beth-horon in Ephraim, now Samaritan territory (a Samaritan, not a Moabite)
from Horonaim, a city of Moab

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the three days as rest and devotion after Ezra's example; Keil lets them open toward the secret night survey, kept quiet because of Sanballat and Tobiah's hostility.
Gill takes the pause as recovery from the journey and the receiving of friends, as Ezra had done (Ezra 8:32).
Keil traces the night route by the valley-gate toward the dragon-well and dung-gate, viewing walls broken down and gates burned; the dragon-well perhaps Gihon.
Henry draws the lessons: good work well considered is well done; leaders should see with their own eyes, not others' reports; those who would build the church's walls must first survey their ruins.
Wesley: the life of his business lay in secrecy and expedition, and he took but one beast to prevent noise.
Gill: the darkness and small company were for secrecy, that no schemes be formed to obstruct the work.
Ellicott sets the valley-gate opening on Hinnom to the south, the dragon-well untraceable, the survey made from the dung port whence offal went to Hinnom.
Clarke explains the dragon-well's figure and the dung port on the east; Wesley notes the footmen led the way as Nehemiah set out to circle the whole city.
Gill takes the valley-gate toward the valley of Jehoshaphat, or the Kidron ravine, with roads issuing from it.

Gill and Ellicott fix the fountain-gate of Siloah, called the king's pool; Keil places it on the eastern slope of Zion and identifies the pool with Josephus's Solomon's pool, weighing the Fountain-of-the-Virgin view.
Clarke guesses the king's pool to be Hezekiah's aqueduct bringing Gihon's waters into the city (2 Chron. 32:30); Wesley explains the impassable way as heaps of rubbish.

sides.position: the reservoir Josephus calls Solomon's pool, east of Siloah
the aqueduct Hezekiah made to bring Gihon's waters into the city of David

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the ride as completing the circuit of the walls; Keil corrects older expositors, taking the Hebrew as a continuous ascent of the valley and a simple re-entry by the valley-gate, not a retracing of the road.
Gill identifies the 'brook' as the Kidron in the eastern ravine.

Keil numbers all left uninformed — Jews, priests, nobles (heads of houses), rulers (town authorities), and the builders; Ellicott justifies the caution, for the city teemed with danger and the rulers had no repressive power.
Clarke: he made no one privy to the design, to hide it from enemies till all was ready; Wesley glosses 'the rest that did the work' as those he meant to employ.
Gill distinguishes the Persian 'rulers' from the Jewish rulers named with the priests and nobles.
Henry finds a model of leadership: Nehemiah joins himself to the people ('let us build'), does not command imperiously, and grounds the call in the special grace of God, not his own authority.
Keil reads the speech as calculated to win favour — the distress set forth, the wall to be built, the reproach removed; Ellicott notes the 'then' marks matured plans, not a fixed time.
Gill identifies the hearers as the priests and princes of the Jews.
Henry hears a whole community kindle — 'many a good work would find hands enough if there were but one good head to lead'; by stirring up one another we strengthen one another for the work.
Clarke: he opened his design and commission; Wesley unfolds 'rise up' as vigour, diligence, and resolution, and 'their hands' as their own and one another's.
Ellicott: he related his providential call with the king's authority, and the people were thoroughly enlisted.
Gill glosses 'the hand of my God' as the providence that exalted him, gave him the king's ear, and inclined the king's heart.

Keil reads the taunt as ironic — they did not credit the Jews with power to fortify and rebel — and places Geshem (Gashmu) as an Arab chief near Jerusalem; Ellicott completes the 'triumvirate,' Tobiah and Geshem in Sanballat's service.
Clarke exposes the malice: 'will ye rebel against the king?' was meant to raise jealousies and induce the king to recall his ordinance.
Gill takes Geshem for an Arabian by birth and governor of a part of Arabia near Judea.
Henry frames the scorn as representing the work both silly and seditious, and hears in it the serpent's seed's enmity, confined to no age or nation.

Keil renders the grave reply and explains the 'memorial' as belonging only to the congregation who live on in their descendants; Ellicott calls it a defiance in the name of the God of heaven, strengthening Zerubbabel's answer.

Clarke: to be a citizen of Jerusalem was a high honour barred to non-Israelites, the very answer Zerubbabel gave the Samaritans (Ezra 4:3); Wesley glosses the three denials of portion, right, and memorial.
Henry draws out the faith beneath the defiance: the Jews bore up as servants of the God of heaven who would prosper them though the heathen raged (Ps. 2:1).
Gill notes he answered with spirit and boldness, unintimidated by scoffs or threats.

themes: the God of heaven will prosper us
